_doc: Built works that are not a carriage mode of their own. type "crossing": a bridge over a river crossing (a land edge between tiles on the same river), recorded on the edge key like a road; with it land modes cross without the ford and a railway can cross at all. type "harbour": a port on a coastal tile with no natural harbour (the map's is_port layer), recorded on the tile id; it joins the tile to the sea edges of the bordering harbours. construction: trade (the wage that pays the work), length_m and section_m2 (the solid volume placed), material and tonnes_per_m3 (what the volume is made of), fixed_materials_tonnes (timber for centring, gates and fittings, per work), person_days_per_m3 (all-in labour: quarrying, dressing, hauling, laying, foundations in water), crew_people and work_days_per_year (how many work at once and how long a year), work_hours_per_day. improvement_node: the tech node that lets an actor build it.

entries.label: Bridge over a river crossing
entries.source: Labelled heuristic: a river crossing of a couple of hundred metres, a masonry bridge six metres wide with piers and arch ring equal to a solid section of a few metres, timber centring; the all-in labour per cubic metre covers quarrying to foundations and is a round figure. Not fitted to a source.
entries.why: What bridging a river costs from the volume of masonry and timber; a stone bridge of this size took years with a crew of over a hundred.

entries.label: Port on a coast tile
entries.source: Labelled heuristic: a mole and quay a few hundred metres long of rubble and cut stone, ten metres wide and six high, with bollards and fittings of timber; the labour per cubic metre is a round figure for rubble laid in water. Not fitted to a source.
entries.why: What opening a coast tile to ships costs from the volume of its mole and quay.
